title: Room-temperature local strain control of moiré excitons in MoS$_2$/WSe$_2$ heterobilayers
authors: T. O. Oskolkova, Y. Koo, A. A. Shubnic, I. Yu. Chestnov, I. Choi, C. Cheng, D. Huang, T. Jiang, K. -D. Park, I. V. Iorsh, V. Kravtsov
abstract: Moiré superlattices in heterobilayers of atomically thin transition metal dichalcogenides provide a versatile platform for exploring quantum many-body physics as they can trap excitons, leading to the formation of quantized moiré exciton states. However, such moiré excitons have been predominantly studied at cryogenic temperatures, which severely limits their practical applications. Here, we demonstrate room-temperature activation and control of moiré excitons in MoS$_2$/WSe$_2$ heterobilayers using local strain engineering. Applying mechanical strain with a modified atomic force microscopy tip, we observe a series of resonances attributed to interlayer exciton states confined in the moiré potential. Power-dependent photoluminescence measurements elucidate the population dynamics of the moiré exciton states, while controlled local strain enables continuous tuning of their emission wavelength to the center of the second telecom window. We provide a theoretical model that captures all experimentally observed features, including the unconventional spectral shape of the moiré exciton emission. Our findings establish local tip-induced strain as a powerful tool for the on-demand manipulation of moiré excitons, paving the way for room-temperature quantum excitonic devices.
summary: This work demonstrates room-temperature control over moiré excitons in $	ext{MoS}_2/	ext{WSe}_2$ heterobilayers by applying local mechanical strain via an AFM tip. By coupling strain engineering with PL spectroscopy and advanced theoretical modeling, the authors show they can not only activate these excitons at ambient temperatures but also tune their emission wavelength into the crucial second telecom window. This establishes local strain as a powerful tool for realizing practical quantum excitonic devices.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is overcoming the limitation of studying moiré excitons at cryogenic temperatures to enable practical, room-temperature quantum control.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that local strain engineering using an AFM tip can activate, control, and tune the emission wavelength of moiré excitons in $	ext{MoS}_2/	ext{WSe}_2$ heterobilayers to the second telecom window at room temperature.
method: The study combines experimental measurements (PL spectroscopy under controlled local strain and power variation) with theoretical modeling (DFT and kinetic rate equations).
model_or_system: The system is the moiré superlattice formed by stacking $	ext{MoS}_2/	ext{WSe}_2$ heterobilayers. The physics involves quantized moiré exciton states whose properties are tuned by external mechanical strain.
key_observables: Photoluminescence (PL) spectra, moiré exciton resonance energies ($	ext{X}1-	ext{X}6$), spectral linewidth, and the effective emission energy as a function of applied strain.
important_parameters: Room temperature (300 K), local strain magnitude (tensile/compressive), excitation power ($P$), and the resulting shift towards the telecom window ($\sim 1.3 \mu	ext{m}$).
main_assumptions: The theoretical model assumes the blueshift is due to repulsive dipole–dipole interactions, and the kinetic model assumes excitation populates the highest energy level followed by non-radiative relaxation.
figures_summary: Figures show the PL spectrum evolving dramatically under increasing strain (multiple resonances emerging), the dependence of peak amplitudes on excitation power, and quantitative plots mapping the effective emission energy against applied strain (showing both initial blueshift and subsequent redshift).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical platform (moiré excitons), details the experimental control mechanism (local strain via AFM), analyzes the spectral signatures (power dependence and strain tuning), and supports these findings with a comprehensive theoretical model capturing the energy shifts and linewidth narrowing.
why_interesting: The ability to use mechanical strain as a non-electrical, on-demand knob to tune quantum optical properties (like emission wavelength) at ambient conditions is highly relevant for developing practical quantum light sources and excitonic devices.
